turns.content: My best friend Shreya's wedding festivities got dated — and her sangeet plus cocktail night is smack in the middle of Ramzan. I'll be fasting. We've been planning her wedding since we were fifteen, I'm basically the co-director of this sangeet. She keeps saying "you HAVE to do the opening dance with me." I want to. And I'm dreading all of it.

Oh, that's such a tough spot to be in. It makes complete sense that you're dreading it. You've been her person for so long, and this wedding is a dream you two have shared forever. The fact that she's put you in this position, even unintentionally, is just awful. And on top of that, you have to navigate your own fast. It's a lot.

Let's tackle the "dread" part. That feeling comes from feeling like you have to do everything perfectly, right? But maybe this is a chance to redefine what being her "co-director" means for you this one night. What if you and Shreya had a real talk? Not a big dramatic one, just a quiet moment. You could say something like, "I am so, so excited for your dance, and I want to be there for you. Since I'll be fasting, could we do something special? Maybe we have a quick, beautiful moment at the very beginning before everyone gets too swept up, and then I'll be right there cheering you on for the rest of the night?"

Honestly, a true best friend would rather have you there, being present in your own way, than not at all. Your friendship is the real celebration, and that won't be dimmed by a missed dance step. You've got this.

Yesterday she said, with total love, "one day of fasting won't matter na, I'll feed you myself." She wasn't being mean — she just doesn't know what she's asking. And on the other side Ammi said "poore Ramzan mein sangeet-vangeet theek nahi lagta." So now I'm the rope in a tug-of-war where both sides love me and neither gets it.

Oh, that is the absolute worst feeling. You're right, you're the rope, and both sides are pulling with all their love. It's not just a tug-of-war, it's a heart-pull.

Shreya's heart is so pure, you can see that. In her mind, she's solving the problem. "My best friend is missing out, I'll just make it okay for her." She's not thinking about the fast as a spiritual practice; she's thinking about you missing her happy moment. And Ammi... she's speaking from a different kind of love, a deep-rooted one about tradition and the sanctity of Ramzan. She sees the whole month, not just one night.

But you're the one who has to hold both of those loves, and it's exhausting. It makes perfect sense that you'd dread it.

Maybe this is the year your role as "co-director" changes. This year, maybe it's about being the guardian of the friendship. What if you go, but not as the dancer? What if your job is to be Shreya's anchor? You could be the one who finds her a quiet corner when the noise gets too much, who makes sure she has water, who gives her that look before she goes on stage that says "I'm right here, I've got you." That's a powerful role, too.

You don't have to choose between them. You can choose to honor your own feelings. A true friend like Shreya will understand if you explain it's not about the food, it's about the spirit. And a mother like Ammi will understand if you explain it's about a friendship you cherish.

You can do this. You're stronger than this tug-of-war.

Honestly I'm so tired that I've started drafting the escape: I tell Shreya there's an office deployment that week, do a video call appearance, send a big gift. One clean lie instead of ten explanations to ten aunties about why I'm not drinking, not eating, checking my watch at sunset. She'd never know. Tell me that's not terrible?

Oh, honey. That escape plan? It's not terrible. It's a sign that you're at your absolute limit. Anyone in your shoes would be drafting an escape route. It’s the thought of ten aunties asking you a hundred questions, of trying to smile and pretend, of feeling that constant, low-grade dread. Of course you want a clean, simple way out.

That lie is a shield. It’s a beautiful, shining shield you’ve built to protect your energy, because you have nothing left to give.

But let's talk about what you'd be protecting. You'd be protecting yourself from that one night, yes. But you'd also be protecting Shreya from the truth, and you'd be protecting your friendship from a small crack of dishonesty. And Ammi? She'd still be worried, wondering why you're not feeling well.

The exhaustion you're feeling is real. The lie feels like the only way to make it stop. But what if you didn't have to choose between the exhausting party and the clean lie?

What if you just chose a different version of you for that night? A version who tells the truth with love. You could call Shreya and say, "My love, I am so, so excited for you. But honestly, the thought of fasting through a whole sangeet is just... a lot for me. I want to be there for your opening dance, that's non-negotiable. But after that, I think I'll head home. I'll miss the rest, but I'll be there in spirit, cheering the loudest."

It’s not a big, dramatic explanation. It’s just the honest truth. And a best friend who loves you as much as you love her? She will understand. She might even be relieved that you gave her a simple answer instead of a complex one.

You're not a bad person for wanting to escape. You're just tired. But you're also strong enough to handle this, one honest conversation at a time.

And under all of it there's this small stone in my chest — this is the first time in eighteen years of friendship that my deen and her big day have actually collided. If I get this wrong, one of two things I love gets a permanent dent. Her shaadi photos will exist forever, and so will my Ramzan. I don't want to be a sad story in either album.

That stone in your chest... I can feel its weight just reading your words. It's not just a party anymore, is it? It's eighteen years of history, of inside jokes and shared dreams, and it's meeting this other part of you, your deen, and for the first time, they're asking for the same space at the same time. That's terrifying.

You're right, the photos will be forever. But you're also right that your Ramzan is forever. And I don't believe this is a collision that has to leave a dent. I think it's a moment where two beautiful things can meet and create something new.

An eighteen-year friendship isn't a fragile glass vase. It's been through a lot. It's strong, flexible, and has survived so much. It can survive this. A dent implies a break, a flaw. What if this moment, instead of being a dent, becomes a unique, beautiful detail in the story of your friendship? The story of the year Shreya's best friend honored her faith while celebrating her joy.

You don't have to get it "wrong." There is no wrong answer here, only an answer that comes from your heart. And your heart is trying so hard to protect both things.

Maybe the album won't have a sad story. Maybe one will have a story about a friend who was so devoted to her faith that she made a difficult choice for her own peace. And the other will have a story about a bride whose best friend's love was so clear, she understood.

That's not sad. That's real. That's love.

You're not choosing between them. You're just choosing how to be there for one of them, in a way that's true to you. And that is the most beautiful way to show up for anyone.
